mainTopic: Attached blades, a fixed knife and pressing, reed-stalk rules, and the משנה's 'הכל שוחטין' and 'לעולם שוחטין'
overview: The גמרא asks whether a blade that was detached and later attached counts as attached for שחיטה. Several proofs from a ברייתא are tried and all are pushed aside: the flint is in a cave wall that was always attached, and a knife stuck in a wall never becomes part of the wall. שמואל then limits the knife-in-the-wall ruling to a knife above the neck, because of the worry of pressing (דרסה). רב זביד and רב פפא each defend שמואל against a ברייתא that seems to allow both positions. Next comes a list of five things you may not do with a reed stalk, and the גמרא narrows or explains several of them. Finally the גמרא explains the משנה's words 'הכל שוחטין' (every animal, even a bird, needs שחיטה) and 'לעולם שוחטין'. רבה ties the second phrase to רבי ישמעאל's view about בשר תאוה staying permitted even after the exile. רב יוסף begins objecting to this, and his objection continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Is a detached-then-attached blade treated as attached for slaughter?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to treat something that was תלוש (detached) and later attached, when it comes to שחיטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If something was detached and in the end someone attached it, what is the law regarding slaughter?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question. If a blade was once loose and then got fixed into the ground, do we treat it as attached (מחובר) or as detached for שחיטה?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already know that a blade growing straight from the ground counts as attached. A totally loose blade counts as detached. This question is about the in-between case: something loose that a person later fixed in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Detached, not connected to the ground

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of this section is an attempt to answer this question from ברייתות.

phrases.english: Detached and in the end he attached it
with regard to slaughter, what is the law?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether something detached and later attached counts as מחובר or as תלוש for שחיטה.

steps.title: First proof: a flint sticking out of a wall
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that slaughtering with a flint sticking out of a wall is invalid. The wall was built from stones that were once loose, so this seems to show that detached-then-attached counts as attached.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If a flint was sticking out of a wall, or a reed was growing up by itself, and he slaughtered with it, his slaughter is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the question. A flint in a wall counts as attached, and the slaughter with it is פסולה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumes the wall is an ordinary built wall. Its stones were once loose and were later attached. Since the ברייתא invalidates the slaughter, detached-then-attached would seem to count fully as מחובר.

keyTerms.meaning: A flint stone, which can have a sharp edge

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If there was a flint sticking out of the wall,
or there was a reed growing up by itself,
and he slaughtered with it, his slaughter is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הָיָה צוֹר יוֹצֵא מִן הַכּוֹתֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a ברייתא as an answer to the question in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That detached-then-attached counts as מחובר for שחיטה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא invalidating slaughter with a flint sticking out of a wall.

steps.title: Rejection: the wall is a cave wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the ברייתא is talking about the wall of a cave, which was never detached.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? With the wall of a cave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the proof away. The flint was part of a cave wall, natural rock that was always attached.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wall was always attached, the ברייתא is simply about something that grew attached. That case was never in doubt. So it teaches us nothing about detached-then-attached.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
The wall of a cave, natural rock that was always attached

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying a flint in a built wall would be kosher. It only says this ברייתא does not prove the point either way.

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
With the wall of a cave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 2 by reading the ברייתא as a different case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the flint in the wall.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed a built wall, but the ברייתא can mean a cave wall that was always attached.

steps.title: The wording supports the cave-wall reading
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא puts the flint next to a reed growing by itself, which was always attached. So the flint must also be something always attached.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also precise, since it teaches it alongside 'a reed growing up by itself.' Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its rejection with a close reading of the ברייתא's own wording, and accepts that reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists the flint together with a reed that grows on its own, which was never detached. Cases listed together are usually alike, so the flint is probably also naturally attached, as in a cave wall. 'שמע מינה' confirms that this reading is right.

keyTerms.meaning: The wording is also precise (it supports this reading)
Learn from it (the point is confirmed)

steps.whatToRemember: The first proof is gone. The flint case is about something that was always attached, so it says nothing about detached-then-attached.

phrases.english: It is also precise,
since it teaches it similar to 'a reed growing up by itself,'
phrases.notes: The reed grew straight from the ground and was never loose, so the flint next to it is understood the same way.

phrases.english: learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rejection in step 3 from the ברייתא's wording.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא is about a cave wall that was always attached.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The flint is listed alongside a reed growing by itself.

steps.title: Second proof: a knife stuck into a wall
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says slaughtering with a knife stuck into a wall is valid. This seems to show that detached-then-attached counts as detached.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If he stuck a knife into a wall and slaughtered with it, his slaughter is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a second proof, this time pointing the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The knife was loose and then got fixed into the wall, a clear case of detached-then-attached. Since the slaughter is כשרה, it would seem such an object is not treated as מחובר.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he stuck a knife into the wall
and slaughtered with it, his slaughter is valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof failed, brings a new ברייתא for the question in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That detached-then-attached counts as תלוש for שחיטה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא validating slaughter with a knife stuck into a wall.

steps.title: Rejection: a knife is never made part of the wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says a knife is different, because a person does not give it up to become part of the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: A knife is different, because he does not make it part of the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the second proof away as well. A knife is a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person sticks a knife into a wall for the moment and plans to pull it out. He never makes it a permanent part of the wall. So it stays detached, and that tells us nothing about an object a person really does attach for good.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives up an object's separate identity so it becomes part of something else

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs were rejected, so the question of detached-then-attached for שחיטה is still open at this point.
steps.confusionAlert: The knife case is kosher only because the knife never became part of the wall. That does not prove that every detached-then-attached object counts as detached.

phrases.english: A knife is different,
because he does not make it part of the wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the knife stuck into the wall.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A knife is never made part of the wall (לא מבטל ליה), so it is a different case from a truly attached object.

steps.title: Another proof from the opening line of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says slaughtering with something attached to the ground is valid. The גמרא suggests this must mean something detached and then attached, so detached-then-attached counts as detached.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if one slaughters with something attached to the ground, his slaughter is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another proof, this time from the opening line of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says 'attached to the ground' is valid, yet later it invalidates a flint that was always attached. So the valid 'attached' case must be something that was detached and later attached. That would show detached-then-attached counts as detached.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
With something attached to the ground,
phrases.notes: Later the same ברייתא invalidates the flint that was always attached, so this valid case must be something attached after it was loose.

phrases.english: his slaughter is valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בִּמְחוּבָּר לַקַּרְקַע שְׁחִיטָתוֹ כְּשֵׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new proof attempt after the knife proof was pushed away in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That something detached and then attached counts as detached.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The opening line of the ברייתא: slaughtering with something attached to the ground is valid.

steps.title: The next line explains what 'attached' means: a knife
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's next line, about a knife stuck in a wall, explains the opening line. A knife is different because a person does not give it up to the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps the ברייתא is explaining itself. What does 'attached to the ground' mean? A knife, which a person does not give up to become part of the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof. It says the 'attached' case in the ברייתא is a knife stuck into a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the 'attached' case is a knife, nothing is proven about ordinary detached-then-attached things. As in step 6, a knife never really becomes part of the wall, because the person does not give it up to the wall. So the question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps; used to push away a proof
It is explaining; the next clause explains the earlier one
Gives up an item so it becomes part of something else

phrases.english: Perhaps it is explaining it:
phrases.notes: He means the next line of the ברייתא, about the knife in the wall, explains the 'attached' case.

phrases.english: What is "attached to the ground"?
A knife, which he does not give up to the wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof itself. The question about detached-then-attached is left unanswered.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The 'attached' case may be a knife, which is a special case that is never given up to the wall.
steps.whatToRemember: All the proofs about detached-then-attached have been pushed away. The question stays open.

steps.title: שמואל: a knife in the wall works only when it is above the neck
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that slaughtering with a knife stuck in a wall is valid. רב ענן in the name of שמואל limits it to when the knife is above and the neck below, because of a worry about pressing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: if one stuck a knife into a wall and slaughtered with it, the slaughter is valid. רב ענן said in the name of שמואל: this is only when the knife is above and the animal's neck is below. But if the knife is below and the neck above, we worry that he may press.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes the ברייתא's knife-in-the-wall ruling, and שמואל limits it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the neck is on top of a fixed knife, the animal's weight may push the neck down onto the blade. Then the cut happens by pressing instead of moving back and forth, which is דרסה. When the knife is above, the person lifts the neck and moves it along the blade, so there is no such worry.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when; a limit on a ruling
Pressing the blade down instead of moving it back and forth; makes שחיטה invalid

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the knife-in-the-wall case is invalid. He is only limiting it to one position, the knife above the neck.

phrases.english: The Master said:
If one stuck a knife into a wall
and slaughtered with it, his slaughter is valid.
Rav Anan said in the name of Shmuel:
They taught this only when the knife is above
and the animal's neck is below,
but if the knife is below
and the animal's neck is above,
we are concerned that he may press.
phrases.notes: Pressing means the neck is pushed down onto the blade instead of being moved back and forth, and that makes the slaughter invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: נָעַץ סַכִּין בַּכּוֹתֶל וְשָׁחַט בָּהּ, שְׁחִיטָתוֹ כְּשֵׁרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the knife-in-the-wall ruling quoted in step 5 and looks at it in its own right.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fixed knife is valid only when it is above the neck. When it is below the neck, we worry about דרסה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a fixed blade raises a practical problem of its own, the risk of pressing, apart from the question of whether it counts as attached.

steps.title: The ברייתא allows both positions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: the ברייתא clearly allows both knife-below-neck-above and knife-above-neck-below.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches: whether the knife is below and the neck above, or the knife is above and the neck below!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's limit with the words of the ברייתא itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא talks about attached blades and lists both positions as valid. That seems to contradict שמואל, who invalidates a fixed knife below the neck.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is taught; a challenge from a teaching
Whether this or that; both cases are included

phrases.english: But it is taught:
whether the knife is below
and the animal's neck is above,
or the knife is above
and the animal's neck is below!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's limit in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that a fixed knife below the neck is a problem.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא, which talks about attached blades, explicitly allows the knife-below position.

steps.title: רב זביד: the ברייתא splits its cases
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד explains that each position goes with a different kind of blade. Knife below is valid only with a detached knife. Knife above is valid even with an attached one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: the ברייתא teaches case by case. Knife below and neck above: with a detached knife. Knife above and neck below: even with an attached knife.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד defends שמואל by reading the ברייתא as matching each position with a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists 'attached or detached' and 'below or above'. רב זביד pairs them. Knife below goes with a detached knife, which the person holds and moves, so there is no pressing. Knife above goes with an attached knife. This fits שמואל exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches case by case; different parts go with different cases
Detached; not fixed to the ground

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said: It is taught case by case:
knife below and the animal's neck above —
with a detached knife;
knife above and the animal's neck below —
even with an attached knife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא: its lists are paired case by case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא allows both positions even for an attached knife.
steps.terutzMaskana: Knife below is allowed only with a detached knife. Knife above is allowed even with an attached knife. שמואל stands.

steps.title: רב פפא: the ברייתא is about a light bird
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא gives another answer. The ברייתא allows a fixed knife below the neck when slaughtering a bird, which is light, so there is no worry about pressing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it is talking about a bird, which is light.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a different answer to the challenge, defending שמואל in another way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's worry comes from the weight of the animal pushing its neck onto the blade. A bird is too light for that, so the ברייתא can allow the knife-below position for a bird even with a fixed knife. שמואל's rule still applies to a heavy animal.
steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: a fixed knife below a heavy animal's neck risks דרסה. רב זביד answers that the knife-below case in the ברייתא is a detached knife. רב פפא answers that it is a light bird.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is talking about a bird, which is light.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the challenge in step 10, alongside רב זביד's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the ברייתא is talking about a light bird.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא allows a fixed knife below the neck for any animal.
steps.terutzMaskana: For a light bird there is no worry about pressing. For a heavy animal שמואל's limit applies.

steps.title: Five things you may not do with a reed stalk
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא in the name of רבי יצחק, or a ברייתא, teaches five forbidden uses of a reed stalk: slaughtering, circumcising, cutting meat, picking teeth, and wiping.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יצחק, and some say a ברייתא taught it: Five things were said about the stalk of a reed. You may not slaughter with it, circumcise with it, cut meat with it, pick your teeth with it, or wipe with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a list of five things you may not do with a sharp reed stalk. The next steps will go through some of these rules one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A reed stalk is sharp enough to cut, so people might use it as a knife. The list says it is not fit for several cutting or cleaning jobs. The teaching itself gives no reasons. The גמרא will test some of the items against other sources and practices.

keyTerms.meaning: The stalk (outer shell) of a reed, which is sharp

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yitzchak said,
and some say it was taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: חֲמִשָּׁה דְּבָרִים נֶאֶמְרוּ בִּקְרוּמִית שֶׁל קָנֶה:
phrases.english: Five things were said about the stalk of a reed:
one may not slaughter with it,
and one may not circumcise with it,
and one may not cut meat with it,
and one may not pick teeth with it,
and one may not wipe with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ בְּמַתְנִיתָא תָּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of a knife stuck in a wall. It stays on the theme of which tools may be used for שחיטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A reed stalk may not be used for slaughtering, circumcising, cutting meat, picking teeth, or wiping.

steps.title: A ברייתא allows slaughtering with a reed stalk
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the first item: another ברייתא says you may slaughter with anything, including a reed stalk.
steps.simpleTranslation: You said one may not slaughter with it. But a ברייתא teaches: One may slaughter with anything, whether with flint, with glass, or with the stalk of a reed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first rule on the list. A different ברייתא openly says a reed stalk is fine for slaughtering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list says no slaughtering with a reed stalk. The other ברייתא names the reed stalk as an approved tool, next to flint and glass. Both sources are talking about the same object, so they seem to contradict each other.

phrases.english: "One may not slaughter with it"?
But it is taught: One may slaughter with anything,
whether with flint or with glass,
or with the stalk of a reed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first item of the list from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one may not slaughter with a reed stalk.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A different ברייתא openly lists a reed stalk as a valid slaughtering tool, so the two sources contradict.

steps.title: The ברייתא means a special marsh reed
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא allowing slaughter is talking about a specific kind of reed from the marsh.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The ברייתא that allows it is talking about a marsh reed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא settles the contradiction. The two sources are talking about different kinds of reeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary reed stalks may not be used for slaughtering, as the list says. The ברייתא that allows a reed stalk means a special marsh reed. So the permission is an exception for one type of reed, and the general rule stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: A specific type of reed that grows in a marsh

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: It refers to a marsh reed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing cases: the two sources are talking about different kinds of reed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to discuss the same reed, so they contradicted.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ordinary reeds are forbidden for slaughter. The marsh reed is allowed.

steps.title: Sages who did cut certain foods with a reed
steps.stepSummary: On the rule not to cut meat with a reed, the גמרא reports that רב פפא cut clear fish innards with it and רבה בר רב הונא cut soft bird meat with it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The list said not to cut meat with it. Yet רב פפא would cut clear fish innards with it, and רבה בר רב הונא would cut soft bird meat with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the third rule, not cutting meat with a reed. It reports how two sages acted, which shows the rule has limits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule does not cover every kind of food. The גמרא points out that the fish innards were clear and the bird meat was soft. These details seem to show why it was safe in those cases: anything stuck in clear innards would be easy to see, and soft meat is easy on the reed. So the ban mainly covers ordinary, tougher meat.

phrases.english: "And one may not cut meat with it."
Rav Pappa would cut with it
fish innards, which are clear.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא מְחַתֵּךְ בַּהּ
phrases.english: Rabbah bar Rav Huna would cut with it
bird meat, which is soft.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מְחַתְּכִין בָּהּ בָּשָׂר. רַב פָּפָּא מְחַתֵּךְ בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the slaughtering rule to the meat-cutting rule of the list in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ban on cutting meat with a reed does not apply to clear fish innards or soft bird meat, as shown by the sages' practice.

steps.title: Why list wiping, if another rule already forbids it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the list needs to forbid wiping with a reed, since a known rule already says wiping with something that can burn is harmful.
steps.simpleTranslation: The list said not to wipe with it. But that should already be clear from what the Master said: Whoever wipes with something that fire can burn, his teeth fall out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the fifth rule, about wiping. That rule seems unneeded, because a different teaching already forbids wiping with anything that burns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A reed burns easily. There is already a general rule that wiping after using the bathroom with anything burnable causes harm. So listing the reed as a special rule adds nothing new, and the challenge is that this item looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Derive it already from (another reason). Asks why a separate rule is needed

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a contradiction between two sources. The גמרא agrees wiping with a reed is bad. It is only asking why the list needs to say it, since another rule already covers it.

phrases.english: "And one may not wipe with it"?
Derive it already from what the Master said:
One who wipes with something that fire can burn,
his teeth fall out.
phrases.notes: Literally "his teeth." This is understood as a polite way of describing harm to the lower part of the body.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מְקַנְּחִין בַּהּ, תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the fifth item of the list in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the list's rule against wiping with a reed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A general rule against wiping with burnable things already covers a reed, so listing it separately seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The list means wiping a wound
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the list's ban on wiping with a reed means cleaning the opening of a wound.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: We are talking about wiping the opening of a wound.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by explaining that the list means a different kind of wiping.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule about burnable things is about wiping after using the bathroom. The list is talking about cleaning a wound with a reed, which that rule does not cover. So the list's item teaches something new and is not extra.

keyTerms.meaning: We are talking about (explains what the text means)

steps.whatToRemember: Each item on the reed list gets narrowed or explained. Slaughtering is forbidden except with a marsh reed. Cutting is allowed for clear fish innards and soft bird meat. Wiping means cleaning a wound.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: קִינּוּחַ פִּי מַכָּה קָאָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: We are talking about wiping the opening of a wound.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: קִינּוּחַ פִּי מַכָּה קָאָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the wiping on the list is a different kind of wiping.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The list seemed to mean wiping after using the bathroom, which another rule already forbids.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list means cleaning a wound with a reed, which is a new rule.

steps.title: Every animal, even a bird, needs slaughter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the phrases 'הכל שוחטין, ולעולם שוחטין' from the משנה and explains that 'הכל שוחטין' means every kind of animal needs שחיטה, even a bird.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'All slaughter, and one may always slaughter.' 'All slaughter' means every animal is included in שחיטה, even a bird.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the next words of the משנה and explains what 'הכל שוחטין' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think 'הכל' means 'all people may slaughter.' The גמרא reads it as 'all animals need slaughter.' This includes a bird, even though one might have thought a bird does not need full שחיטה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'All slaughter'; here it means all animals need שחיטה

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'הכל' is about which animals need שחיטה. It is not about which people are allowed to slaughter.

phrases.english: All slaughter, and one may always slaughter.
phrases.notes: These words are quoted from our משנה.

phrases.english: "All slaughter" means:
all are included in slaughter, and even a bird.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַכֹּל שׁוֹחֲטִין – הַכֹּל בִּשְׁחִיטָה, וַאֲפִילּוּ עוֹף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the reed discussion, the גמרא moves on to the next phrases of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every kind of animal needs שחיטה, including a bird.

steps.title: Who holds 'one may always slaughter'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא is the source for the phrase 'לעולם שוחטין'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'One may always slaughter': which תנא taught this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks whose opinion the phrase 'לעולם שוחטין' reflects. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Why would anyone think slaughtering is ever not allowed? The phrase suggests there was a reason to worry about this. So the גמרא looks for the תנא who had that worry.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One may always slaughter', at all times and in every era
'Who is the תנא?', asking whose opinion this is

phrases.english: "One may always slaughter": who is the one who taught it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining the first phrase, the גמרא asks about the second phrase.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's view the phrase 'לעולם שוחטין' follows, and why it needed to be said.

steps.title: רבה: it is רבי ישמעאל, who says the verse permits ordinary meat
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the phrase follows רבי ישמעאל. He reads the פסוק about expanding the borders as permitting בשר תאוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: it is רבי ישמעאל. A ברייתא teaches on the פסוק 'When ה׳ your God expands your border, as He promised you, and you say: I will eat meat...' that רבי ישמעאל says: the verse comes only to permit them ordinary meat.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה names רבי ישמעאל as the source. He quotes a ברייתא where רבי ישמעאל says the פסוק is there to permit ordinary meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל reads the פסוק as a new permission: from now on you may eat meat just because you want it. If it is a new permission, it must have been forbidden before. That is the background the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Meat of desire': ordinary meat eaten because one wants it, not as a קרבן
'The verse comes only to...', saying what the פסוק's purpose is

phrases.english: Rabba said: It is Rabbi Yishmael,
as it is taught:
"When the Lord your God expands your border
as He has spoken to you,
and you say: I will eat meat, etc."
Rabbi Yishmael says:
The verse comes only
to permit them meat of desire.
phrases.notes: Meaning plain meat a person eats because he wants it, not meat from a קרבן.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of who the תנא is.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase follows רבי ישמעאל, who holds that the פסוק newly permitted בשר תאוה.

steps.title: Ordinary meat: forbidden at first, permitted in the Land
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains that ordinary meat was forbidden at first and became permitted when the people entered ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first, ordinary meat was forbidden to them. Once they entered the Land, ordinary meat was permitted to them.
steps.whatsHappening: This continues רבי ישמעאל's words. It gives the history behind the permission: first forbidden, then permitted on entering the Land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key point is that the permission came at a specific moment, when they entered ארץ ישראל. Because the permission is linked to that event, it raises the question of what happens if that situation ends.

phrases.english: For at first, meat of desire was forbidden to them;
once they entered the Land,
meat of desire was permitted to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the background of רבי ישמעאל's reading of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בשר תאוה was forbidden in the מדבר and permitted once the people entered ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: Even after exile, slaughtering ordinary meat stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: Since the permission began when the people entered the Land, one might think the ban returns after the exile. The משנה says 'לעולם שוחטין' to teach that it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that they were exiled, might they go back to their original prohibition? That is why we learned: one may always slaughter.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה ties everything back to the משנה. 'לעולם שוחטין' teaches that ordinary meat stays permitted even after the exile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי ישמעאל's view, the permission came with entering the Land. So losing the Land might seem to bring back the old ban. The word 'לעולם' rules that out: slaughtering for ordinary meat is permitted in every era.

keyTerms.meaning: 'One might think', bringing up a possible mistaken idea

steps.whatToRemember: 'הכל שוחטין' means every animal, even a bird, needs שחיטה. According to רבה, 'לעולם שוחטין' follows רבי ישמעאל: ordinary meat was permitted when the people entered the Land, and this permission stays even after the exile. רב יוסף challenges this reading in the next steps.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'לעולם' means 'at all times, in every era'. It does not mean 'with any tool'; that was the earlier phrase 'ובכל שוחטין'.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains why the משנה needed the extra phrase 'לעולם שוחטין': to make sure no one thinks the exile took away permission to eat ordinary meat.

phrases.english: And now that they were exiled,
might one think they go back to their original prohibition?
Therefore we learned: One may always slaughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the history of בשר תאוה to explain why the משנה says 'לעולם שוחטין'.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Following רבי ישמעאל, the משנה teaches that permission to slaughter ordinary meat stays in force forever, even after the exile.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רבה, 'לעולם שוחטין' follows רבי ישמעאל. It teaches that the permission for בשר תאוה, which began on entering the Land, does not end with the exile.

steps.title: רב יוסף: The משנה Should Have Said 'Slaughter and Eat'
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף attacks רבה's reading. If the משנה were teaching that בשר תאוה stays permitted forever, it should have said 'לעולם שוחטין ואוכלין', because the issue is eating the meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף objected: If so, this phrase 'One may always slaughter' is not the right wording. It should have said 'One may always slaughter and eat'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges רבה's explanation by pointing to the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי ישמעאל's view, what was forbidden in the מדבר was eating ordinary meat, not slaughtering an animal. So a משנה teaching that this permission lasts forever should talk about eating. Since the משנה says only 'שוחטין' (slaughter), רב יוסף argues it is not talking about רבי ישמעאל's issue at all.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it: a strong challenge to an explanation

steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף is not arguing with the משנה itself. He is arguing with רבה's explanation of why the משנה says 'לעולם שוחטין'.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef objects to it:
phrases.notes: He is objecting to רבה's explanation from step 21, that this phrase follows רבי ישמעאל.

phrases.english: This phrase "One may always slaughter"
should have said "One may always slaughter and eat"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation from steps 21 to 23 that 'לעולם שוחטין' teaches that בשר תאוה stays permitted after the exile.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that 'לעולם שוחטין' follows רבי ישמעאל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The permission in רבי ישמעאל's view is about eating, so the משנה's wording should mention eating. Since it mentions only slaughtering, it does not fit that reading.

steps.title: רב יוסף's Second Objection: The Reason Was Closeness to the משכן
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף adds a second challenge. He looks at why the meat was forbidden at first and why it was later permitted. The answer is being near the משכן versus being far from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: at first, why was it forbidden? Because they were close to the משכן. And in the end, why was it permitted? Because they were far from the משכן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף opens a second objection by first spelling out the reason behind the ban and the permission. This is a setup line, and his actual point comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban in the מדבר depended on living close to the משכן. The permission in ארץ ישראל depended on living far from it. So the permission was never tied to being in the Land itself. That is why the worry that the ban returns after the exile seems baseless: the people are even farther from the משכן then.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore: introduces an additional objection

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the reason behind a law decides when the law applies. If closeness to the משכן caused the ban, then being in or out of the Land does not matter.

phrases.english: And furthermore,
at first, what is the reason it was forbidden?
Because they were close to the Tabernacle.
And in the end, what is the reason it was permitted?
Because they were far from the Tabernacle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, logic-based objection after the wording objection in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea from step 23 that one might think the ban on בשר תאוה returns after the exile
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ban and the permission depended on distance from the משכן, not on entering the Land. After the exile the people are still far away, so there was never any reason to think the ban returns.
